/case-studies/meridian-expense-approvals.title: Approval flow redesign — Case Study
/case-studies/meridian-expense-approvals.description: How an eight-state accountability model cut median expense approval time from 3.2 days to 29 hours for a B2B finance SaaS.
p: Meridian
Role
Lead Product Designer
Duration
8 months
Team
Squad of 7 - product manager, five engineers, me

Every Thursday, Meridian's biggest customer ran the same ritual: a finance manager opened a spreadsheet, cross-referenced it against our product, and chased approvers on Slack one by one. Our product was the system of record, and it was being managed from outside itself.
Expense requests didn't fail in Meridian. They stalled - for a median of 3.2 days - because at any given moment nobody could say whose turn it was.
Median time to approval: 3.2 days down to 29 hours
Feature satisfaction score after relaunch, up from 4.6 out of 10
Task completion in moderated usability testing, up from 61% on the old flow
Approval-related support tickets in the first quarter after launch
Escalation by design

Silence is a state, so it got designed like one. Every wait has a clock, every clock has a consequence, and every consequence names its new owner. Stalling stopped being invisible - which is why it stopped.
State is the interface

Every screen answers three questions before anything else: what state is this request in, who owns the next move, and what happens if they don't move. If a surface couldn't answer all three, it didn't ship.
Density is a feature

Approvers are repeat expert users, not first-time visitors. The queue is a keyboard-first table with bulk actions, not a friendly card feed. We optimised for the fortieth approval of the session, not the first.
What I owned

I owned the approval state model - the eight states, their owners, and their timeouts - which became the contract between design, engineering, and the finance customers themselves. The flows, the queue design, the escalation UX, and the email digest interaction were mine end to end.
I also ran the research: 14 approver interviews across 6 customers, 3 rounds of moderated testing, and the diary study that surfaced the batching behaviour the whole design ultimately serves.
Original brief
Redesign the expense approval screens to match the new brand and reduce the number of clicks it takes to approve a request.

The brief assumed the problem was friction on the approval screen. It wasn't. Session recordings showed approvers spent under nine seconds on the approve action itself - and days not opening the product at all.
Requests stalled between people, not inside screens. The flow had no owner, no deadline, and no consequence for inaction. Fewer clicks on a screen nobody visits changes nothing.
The reframe
Design the approval flow around accountability: at every moment, exactly one person owns the next step, they know it, and something defined happens if they don't act.
The first six weeks produced no screens - an approval state model, an ownership matrix, and an escalation policy instead. Every surface we shipped afterwards is a projection of that model.
Approvers batched their work into two or three 20-minute sessions per week.

The diary study killed the notification-per-request model. The queue became a batch-triage table - bulk select, keyboard shortcuts, policy pre-checks - so a 20-minute session clears 40 requests instead of 12.
68% of rejected requests were resubmitted completely unchanged.
Rejection wasn't communicating. We made 'reject' impossible without a structured reason, and the resubmission form arrives with the problem pre-highlighted. Unchanged resubmissions fell to 9%.
Managers acted on email three times more often than they opened the app.
Instead of fighting the inbox, we made it a first-class surface: a daily digest where within-policy requests approve in one click, and anything risky links back into the full-context app view.
Employees in their first month caused 70% of policy violations.

Policy was being taught by rejection - the most expensive classroom there is. Policy hints moved to submission time, checking live as the form is filled. Violations from new employees dropped by more than half.
A mobile-first rebuild

Analytics showed 84% of approvals happened at a desk, batched into two or three sessions a week. Mobile was a companion moment - travel and urgencies - not the primary surface. We built it second, deliberately small.
Auto-approval under a threshold

Finance teams told us the audit trail was the product. Removing a human from low-value approvals before trust existed would have poisoned the relationship with the exact stakeholders whose adoption we needed. We shipped one-click - not zero-click - approvals.
A Kanban board metaphor

Prototype testing showed drag-and-drop implied a control approvers don't have: requests move between states by policy, not by hand. Two of six testers tried to drag a card to skip a required step. The metaphor promised the wrong physics.
Approvals inside Slack

A Slack-native prototype doubled the error rate on policy-flagged requests - approvers lost the receipt, the history, and the flags the moment they left the product. Slack kept notification duty; the decision stayed where the context lives.
Progressive disclosure of detail

The pattern-book answer for dense tables. Testing said the opposite: approvers are expert users who wanted more per screen, not less. Hiding the receipt behind a click slowed every decision by seconds that compound at 40 approvals per session.
The queue is built for the fortieth approval of a session, not the first. Bulk select, keyboard shortcuts, and a live policy pre-check mean a 20-minute batch clears 40 requests.
The 'NEXT' column is the accountability model made visible: every row names whose move it is.
The approval queue - a keyboard-first triage table.
Six weeks of the project produced only this: eight states, each with an owner and a clock. Every screen that follows is a projection of this diagram.
The v4 approval state model. Every state names an owner; every wait names a deadline.
The detail view leads with the timeline, not the receipt. Whose turn it is, how long they've had it, and what happens at the 24-hour mark - answered before any evidence is shown.
Approve is one action. Reject cannot be clicked without a structured reason.
Request detail with the ownership timeline front and centre.
The v3 flow buried submission under four stacked modals, and state lived nowhere - completion sat at 61%. Policy failures surfaced only at the end, as rejections.
Submission flow, v3 versus v4.
v4 is a single rail: policy checks resolve live while the form is filled, and routing is visible before submission. Completion rose to 94%, and 'first-month' policy violations fell by more than half.

A small, hard-working kit: seven status chips, three button weights, one dense table spec, and six colour tokens. Status colour is never decorative - green, amber, and red are reserved exclusively for state.
The component kit - status is the only thing allowed to have colour.
Managers acted on email three times more often than they opened the app - so email became a designed surface. Within-policy requests approve in one click; anything flagged links back to full context.
The daily digest: one-click approval for the safe cases, full context for the rest.
Mobile handles exactly two jobs - the urgent approval and the travel check-in - and refuses the rest. 84% of approvals happen at a desk; the phone app is deliberately a companion, not a port.
The mobile companion: two jobs, done fast.
Median approval time fell from 3.2 days to 29 hours, and not a single request has been lost in a stall since launch. The month-five inflection in the chart is the v4 ship date.
Twelve months of cycle-time data. The system did what the model promised.
Four months in, the engineering lead proposed shipping the visual refresh first and the flow changes 'in a fast follow'. The skin was low-risk and demo-ready; the state model touched every service.

I argued we had exactly one credibility window with finance teams: relaunch with the same stalls in a prettier shell, and no one would believe the second launch. I brought the prototype test data - the skin-only variant moved task completion by two points, the full flow by thirty-three - and we held the release. It shipped once, whole.
The design work that mattered here never rendered a pixel: an eight-state model and an ownership rule. Screens, emails, and the mobile app are just projections of it.
This is what I want to be hired for - not the queue table, but the decision that accountability was the product, and the discipline to hold that position through an 8-month delivery.

/case-studies/bitcoin-magazine-ukraine.title: Illustration system — Case Study
/case-studies/bitcoin-magazine-ukraine.description: How a 14-category visual taxonomy replaced a two-hour production bottleneck with a 25-minute pipeline at daily editorial scale.
p: Bitcoin Magazine Ukraine
Role
Art Director
Duration
13 months
Team
2-person creative operation

The lead editor made the same decision every morning: which stories got illustrations and which went out bare. Not because she didn’t care about the uncovered stories — because each illustration took two hours, and the publication was running eight to ten stories a day.
Per-asset production time reduced: 2 hours down to 25 minutes
Assets shipped at publication quality over 13 months
Subscriber growth in the first six months after implementation
Tone accuracy
Brand recognition comes from editorial intelligence, not visual uniformity. A satirical piece and a regulatory analysis shouldn't look alike. Sameness is just recognizable mediocrity.
The taxonomy
At volume, the real design system is the content taxonomy. The 14 categories decided each story's visual treatment before a single stroke. Get the category right and the illustration follows.
Speed is a design constraint
The 25-minute target came before any design work. Strong concepts that took 40 minutes got cut. Speed was a design decision, not a compromise.
What I owned

I owned the content categorization logic, the visual archetype system, the template architecture, and all illustration direction. Every illustration across those 3,000+ assets was produced by me, within the system I had built.

The most important artifacts were not illustrations. They were two documents: the category taxonomy and the template library — Illustrator source files with shared symbol libraries and export presets calibrated for Telegram, web headers, and Instagram formats.
Original brief
Design a visual identity system for Bitcoin Magazine Ukraine’s digital content, adapted from the global Bitcoin Magazine brand.

The brief treated the situation as aesthetic — inconsistent brand application and the wrong tone. The real problem was operational: full visual coverage of daily content required sixteen to twenty hours of illustration time at the existing two-hour-per-piece rate.
That is not a visual identity problem. It is a math problem.
The reframe
Build editorial infrastructure that makes visual quality achievable at daily speed for a two-person creative operation.
The first four weeks produced zero illustrations — a content taxonomy, template architecture, and production constraints instead. By month three, the team shipped eight illustrated pieces a day.
Custom illustration generated 40% higher engagement than photography.
I pulled this from historical content before making any recommendation. It ended the stock-photography conversation and established the investment case for building an illustration pipeline.
The competitor visual field was essentially unoccupied by high-quality illustration.
A content audit across CoinDesk, Decrypt, and the main Ukrainian crypto publications confirmed the illustration-first approach as a genuine differentiation move, not a stylistic preference.
Dark mode performance was not secondary for this audience.
Five pieces designed light-first and adapted to dark performed below the engagement average. The rule: every template built dark-first, with light as the derivative.
A single unified visual style

There was no single visual language that works for market-analysis satire, breaking regulatory news, educational content, and weekly editorial recap without compromising all four. I prioritised meaning and accuracy in every illustration.
Stock photography
Custom illustration generated 38% higher click-through than photography across comparable story types. Stock would have traded the publication’s distinctive visual voice for marginal time savings.
Illustrating without a system

From-scratch illustration has a ceiling of two hours per piece. The answer to “we cannot keep up” was not more illustrators — it was a system where conceptual work happened once at the archetype level.

The cover run treated the magazine as a physical object: an isometric render of the printed issue with dimensional coins beside it. Showing the artifact - paper, spine, shadow - positioned a digital-first publication in the material world.
One angle, one light source, one background color per issue. The template made every cover recognizable at feed size before a single word was read.
Selling a digital publication with the language of print. The object is the brand.

A single figure in a coral-red field, navigating geometric terrain of varying heights, replaced the default candlestick-and-arrow treatment. The coral-red signals danger and opportunity simultaneously; the samurai reads as discipline under pressure.
The key decision was deliberate under-determination: a symbol flexible enough to carry multiple market narratives without a new concept per piece, while remaining immediately identifiable.
The samurai works as a recurring archetype because the symbolism is not specific enough to be wrong for any given market condition. Reusability was the design requirement, not the happy accident.

For coverage of ETFs, exchanges, and government bodies, Bitcoin symbolism was placed inside institutional frames — architectural minimalism, building forms, clean geometric overlays — rather than in opposition to them.

This is a choice about what an image argues. Institutional imagery with Bitcoin inside it says adoption; a logo challenging an institution says conflict. The image makes the editorial argument before the reader sees the headline.

Every image places the Bitcoin symbol inside the institutional frame rather than outside it. The publication’s thesis was adoption. An image that contradicts the text is a liability, not a design choice.

For enforcement and regulation stories, the visual borrows the language of the institution itself - a federal seal, redrawn around the Bitcoin mark. The joke lands because the craft is straight: real seal proportions, real engraving weight.
Satire in this system is never a style break. It reuses the institutional templates at full fidelity, so the same reader trusts the serious pieces.
Parody drawn with the same rigor as the serious work - that is what keeps it from reading as a throwaway meme.

The stars-and-stripes field is reduced to a single repeating star pattern in the publication blue, with Liberty holding the coin against it. State symbolism is quoted, not photographed - the illustration stays inside the established vector language.
Flat pattern left, focal figure center-right: the composition reserves a clean column for the headline by design.
National symbolism translated into the system vocabulary instead of stock imagery.
The satire category had to land specific references for crypto-native readers while remaining legible as humor for those who would not catch them, using typographic displacement and visual puns.

This template was deliberately the least constrained in the system. The 25-minute constraint applied fully, but the design constraints were kept loose by choice — meme culture requires responsiveness to what happened yesterday.
The most under-specified template in the system. If a meme format has too many rules, you have killed the thing that makes it work.

Recurring price-prediction coverage got a card grid: portrait, name, and the number they called, with the price repeating as a typographic ribbon. The format scales - every new prediction is one more card, not one more concept.
Faces are posterized into the two-tone palette so photography sits inside the illustrated system instead of breaking it.
A repeatable format for a repeatable story. The system absorbs photography by reducing it to the palette.
The retrospective stitches archive pieces into a film-strip collage under the Mt. Gox wordmark, muted behind a scrim so the assembled history reads as one image rather than ten.
The scrim is part of the layout: it dims the collage to hold overlay text, which is why this template pairs with a bottom caption instead of fighting the artwork.
Ten stories compressed into one frame - the dimming layer is what makes it usable as a background.
Draft copy - Dan to write.
Draft caption - Dan to write.
Draft copy 2 - Dan to write.
Community archetypes drawn as a hero lineup - phoenix, pirate, samurai - each carrying the coin somewhere in their silhouette. One shared horizon line keeps eight characters reading as a single cast.
Each figure was built to survive being cropped out alone for social, so the group shot doubles as a sprite sheet.
One illustration, nine assets. Group compositions were always drawn for disassembly.
The mining feature sets its headline into the sky and builds the story into the mountain: each silhouetted figure on the slope is a different miner archetype, with the coin embedded in the rock face.
Type and illustration share one grid - the headline is part of the drawing, not a label on top of it.
The composition holds its own title. Layouts like this go to the caption-bottom template so nothing collides.

Two spot illustrations on a neutral field: the miner hoisting the coin as a kettlebell, and the block dragged like a monolith. Paired spots let one screen carry two metaphors without building two scenes.
The empty center strip is deliberate - it is where the connecting copy sits.
Spot pairs are the cheapest unit in the system: two ideas, one screen, space for text built in.

For store-of-value pieces, the coin becomes bullion: a gold-stamped BTC plate rendered with soft dimensionality against flat orange. One object, off-center, with the left half of the frame left empty.
The asymmetry is the template - object right, argument left. It is the fastest layout in the system to produce.
A single well-lit object beats a busy scene when the concept is one word.
The confiscation story runs as a stamped-evidence collage: treasure chests, escaping horses, and the CONFISCATED overprint tying panels together. The stamp motif carries the editorial judgment.
Panels reuse existing category art - the special-issue look is achieved through arrangement and overprint, not new illustration.
Special issues remix the archive instead of commissioning new art. The overprint does the framing.
The weekly recap needed to communicate total editorial scope. The solution was cinematic composition: wide-field scenes with multiple symbolic elements arranged into a single coherent image.
The visual distinction between a recap and a daily piece needs to be legible from a thumbnail.
Milestones get a trophy vignette and a large blank panel - and the panel is the layout: results copy drops into the reserved white field without touching the illustration.
Isometric perspective matches the cover language, so celebration screens still read as part of the same issue.
The empty panel is the design. Reserved text zones let screens be filled without breaking them.
Three months into delivery, the Creative Director told me the system was producing brand fragmentation, and wanted to consolidate 14 categories into four or five.

My counter-argument was six weeks of engagement data and an operational case: consolidation would loosen production constraints and break the 25-minute target. We kept 14 categories and added consistent logo and typographic treatment across all of them.

The hardest part was not the illustration. It was convincing a publication to treat visual production as editorial infrastructure, and holding that position long enough for the system to deliver results visible to everyone in the room.

Infrastructure work that produces nothing visible for weeks is harder to defend than work that ships daily. Defending it requires translating the long-term operational payoff into the commercial terms the decision-maker is actually tracking.
